case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, when a county forecloses on and sells a home to satisfy a small tax debt, the Constitution requires compensation measured by the property’s fair market value (or other metric) rather than limiting the owner to only the post-sale “surplus proceeds,” and whether retaining the owner’s equity can also constitute an excessive fine.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. V (Takings Clause: “nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation”); U.S. Const. amend. VIII (Excessive Fines Clause) as implicated by the tax-foreclosure equity-retention practice.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that the county effected a taking when it acquired/retained the owner’s home equity to satisfy a comparatively tiny delinquent-tax obligation, and that “just compensation” cannot be defined by a bright-line rule equating the owner’s constitutional entitlement with whatever “surplus proceeds” remain after the county conducts its chosen sale process—especially where the home’s fair market value vastly exceeds the tax debt and the government’s sale yields a depressed price. Petitioner further contends that, at least in these circumstances, the government’s retention of substantial equity beyond what is owed is constitutionally suspect and may also function as punishment grossly disproportional to the underlying tax delinquency (raising an Excessive Fines issue). In short: the county must account for the owner’s equity interest and cannot use its own sale mechanics as a categorical valuation shield.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Isabella County) defends the Sixth Circuit’s approach that the Constitution does not guarantee the owner fair market value; instead, the owner is entitled at most to any “surplus proceeds” left after a tax-foreclosure sale satisfies the delinquent taxes, interest, penalties, and costs. The county’s theory treats the auction result as the best (and administrable) evidence of value and seeks to avoid constitutionalizing challenges to the adequacy/fairness of state tax-foreclosure procedures. The county also resists extending the Excessive Fines Clause, portraying the case as one about debt collection and property-value realization rather than punitive forfeiture, and arguing that any process objections (e.g., sale mechanics, timing, or order-of-asset liquidation) sound in due process/state law rather than federal takings or excessive-fines doctrine.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that Tyler protected only the historical “overplus” and did not constitutionalize a fair-market-value floor—reinforces my reluctance to adopt any rigid FMV rule or to turn every depressed tax-sale price into a federal Takings claim. But Justice Kagan rightly identifies the core flaw in the Sixth Circuit’s approach: treating whatever “surplus proceeds” happen to remain after the government’s own compelled-sale mechanics as conclusive just compensation lets the State define away the surplus-equity interest Tyler recognized as property. Justice Jackson’s invocation of New River Collieries and Jacobs underscores that compensation cannot be stipulated by the taker’s chosen mechanism, yet it does not require us to announce an across-the-board valuation metric; the minimal path is to reject the categorical surplus-proceeds-as-compensation rule and remand for a constitutionally meaningful accounting of the owner’s state-defined equity interest. BFP’s forced-sale discount logic remains a practical caution, but it cannot operate as a Fifth Amendment safe harbor where the government both structures the sale and benefits from any suppression of value.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that Tyler protected only the historical “overplus” and did not constitutionalize a fair-market-value floor, so the Takings Clause should not become a general adequacy review of tax-sale prices. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan correctly identify the fatal flaw in the Sixth Circuit’s categorical rule: it allows the State’s own compelled-sale mechanics to define away the very residual equity interest that state law recognizes as the owner’s “property,” which conflicts with the original public meaning of “property” as including the owner’s remaining equity after satisfaction of taxes and costs. New River Collieries and Jacobs (as Justice Jackson notes) reinforce that just compensation cannot be set by the taker’s preferred mechanism, even if they do not mandate an across-the-board FMV test here. BFP remains noncontrolling because it construed a bankruptcy statute’s “reasonably equivalent value,” not the Fifth Amendment’s constraint when the government structures the sale and then claims the depressed proceeds conclusively measure what it took.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan make a serious point that a State should not be able to “define away” an owner’s residual equity interest by designing sale mechanics that predictably yield no surplus, and I agree that BFP’s bankruptcy holding cannot be treated as a categorical Fifth Amendment safe harbor. But that critique does not supply Petitioner’s affirmative Takings theory here, because Tyler framed the protected property as the historical “overplus” after lawful taxes, penalties, and costs—not a constitutional guarantee that a compelled tax sale must clear some appraisal-based floor. Justice Jackson’s invocation of New River Collieries and Jacobs usefully underscores that the government cannot stipulate “just compensation,” yet those cases still assume the taking of a cognizable property interest and do not convert allegedly value-depressing collection procedures into a per se taking absent a showing that the State has appropriated an owner-recognized residual equity interest. Under a restrained textualist approach attentive to practical consequences, I would not constitutionalize foreclosure-price adequacy via the Takings Clause on this record, leaving valuation-method and process concerns to state law and due process frameworks.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that Tyler spoke in terms of an historical “overplus,” not a federal fair-market-value guarantee—rightly cautions against turning every low forced-sale price into a Takings claim. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, the Sixth Circuit’s categorical rule goes too far the other way by letting the government’s own sale mechanics conclusively define the value of the very residual equity interest Tyler recognized, a move that will predictably disadvantage unsophisticated and resource-constrained homeowners. Justice Jackson’s invocation of New River Collieries and Jacobs reinforces my concern: even if we do not constitutionalize a single FMV metric, “just compensation” cannot be whatever the taker’s chosen process happens to yield when the State designs and controls the compelled sale. The pragmatic, narrow remedy is to vacate and remand to reject the per se surplus-proceeds-as-compensation rule, leaving the valuation method and any due process/Eighth Amendment questions for development below.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that Tyler protects the historical “overplus” and does not constitutionalize a fair-market-value floor—still matters, and it cautions against converting every low tax-sale price into a Takings claim. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett now emphasize, the Sixth Circuit’s categorical rule that whatever “surplus proceeds” remain after the government’s chosen sale mechanics conclusively equals just compensation would let the State define away the owner’s retained equity interest Tyler recognizes, especially where the sale design predictably suppresses surplus to zero. BFP cannot do the work the Sixth Circuit assigns it because, as Roberts notes, it interpreted a bankruptcy statute’s “reasonably equivalent value,” not the Fifth Amendment measure of compensation when the government both controls the compelled sale and keeps the residual. The pragmatic middle remains to reject the categorical surplus-proceeds-as-compensation rule and remand for a constitutionally meaningful accounting of the owner’s residual equity interest without announcing an across-the-board FMV mandate or reaching the Eighth Amendment.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that Tyler protected the historical “overplus” and did not constitutionalize an appraisal-based fair-market-value floor; as a textualist, I agree the Fifth Amendment does not mandate any single valuation metric in every tax sale. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan rightly show why the Sixth Circuit’s categorical rule still fails: letting the State’s own compelled-sale mechanics conclusively define “surplus proceeds” as just compensation allows the taker to set the value of the very property interest (residual equity) state law recognizes and Tyler treats as protected. BFP, as Justice Thomas emphasizes, interpreted a bankruptcy statute’s “reasonably equivalent value” and cannot be converted into a Fifth Amendment safe harbor when the government both structures the sale and benefits from any systematic suppression of value. The appropriate disposition remains to reject the conclusive surplus-proceeds rule and remand for a constitutionally meaningful accounting of the owner’s retained equity interest without announcing a rigid FMV requirement.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that Tyler protected only the historical “overplus,” not a federal fair-market-value floor, and we should not turn the Takings Clause into a roving audit of state foreclosure pricing; I agree with that caution. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, the Sixth Circuit went too far the other way by adopting a categorical rule that the County’s own forced-sale “surplus proceeds” conclusively equal just compensation, which risks letting the government define away the very equity interest Tyler recognized as property. BFP’s forced-sale logic (raised by Alito/Barrett) is a practical warning about depressed prices, but it arose in bankruptcy under a statutory “reasonably equivalent value” standard and cannot operate as a constitutional safe harbor when the government controls the sale mechanics and then keeps the residual value. The institutional, minimalist course is to vacate that categorical rule and remand for a constitutionally meaningful accounting of the owner’s retained equity interest without announcing that FMV is always required.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that Tyler protected the historical “overplus” and did not constitutionalize a fair-market-value floor—remains right and continues to counsel against turning every low tax-sale price into a federal takings claim. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively show why the Sixth Circuit’s categorical “surplus proceeds always equals just compensation” rule is untenable as a matter of text and structure: it permits the State to use its own compelled-sale mechanics to define away the very residual equity interest that state law recognizes and Tyler treats as property. Justice Jackson’s reliance on New River Collieries and Jacobs doesn’t push me to adopt a freestanding FMV mandate, but it reinforces that the taker cannot stipulate the constitutional measure of compensation by pointing to the output of its chosen process. I therefore remain with Petitioner to vacate/reverse and remand for a constitutionally meaningful valuation/accounting of the owner’s retained equity interest, without prescribing a single valuation method or resolving due process/Eighth Amendment theories.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that Tyler protects an “overplus” interest and does not constitutionalize a fair-market-value floor—remains right as far as it goes, and it counsels against turning every low tax-sale price into a federal takings claim. But it does not answer the narrower defect identified by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan: the Sixth Circuit’s categorical rule makes the government’s own compelled-sale output conclusive of “just compensation,” effectively letting the State define away the very residual equity interest Tyler recognizes as property. BFP’s bankruptcy context, as multiple colleagues note, provides practical caution about forced-sale discounts but cannot serve as a Fifth Amendment safe harbor when the government designs the process and then keeps whatever value that process suppresses. A pragmatic remedy consistent with procedural fairness is to vacate that categorical rule and remand for an accounting that meaningfully captures the owner’s protected equity without prescribing a single valuation metric or reaching due process/Eighth Amendment issues now.

John Roberts.reasoning: Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023) unanimously held that the taxpayer retains a state-defined property interest in the equity/surplus value beyond the tax debt, and that the government’s retention of that value after satisfying the debt implicates the Takings Clause, U.S. Const. amend. V. The Sixth Circuit’s categorical rule (invoking BFP v. Resolution Trust Corp. (1994)) that “surplus proceeds always equals just compensation” sweeps too broadly because BFP addressed bankruptcy valuation and does not constitutionalize depressed tax-sale prices as a conclusive measure of what was taken. A narrow disposition consistent with institutional restraint is to vacate the categorical rule and require the State to account for the owner’s protected equity interest (as recognized in Tyler and echoed in Rafaeli) rather than using its chosen sale mechanics as an absolute valuation shield. Because the case can be resolved on Takings grounds, I would not reach the Excessive Fines question under the Eighth Amendment.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Fifth Amendment prohibits government from taking “private property” for public use “without just compensation,” and the original public meaning of “property” included the owner’s equity remaining after taxes, penalties, and costs were satisfied. Under Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023), the State may collect the tax debt through seizure and sale, but it may not appropriate the surplus value for itself; treating whatever “surplus proceeds” happen to remain after the County’s chosen forced-sale process as the constitutional measure of compensation invites manipulation and cannot define away the protected property interest. BFP v. Resolution Trust Corp. addressed federal bankruptcy avoidance and does not establish a Fifth Amendment rule that a tax-foreclosure auction price conclusively equals just compensation for the equity taken. Because the County’s retention of substantial equity beyond the debt is an uncompensated appropriation of a vested property interest, the judgment should be reversed at least as to the categorical “surplus proceeds” rule, with any further issues (including any Excessive Fines theory) considered consistent with the Constitution’s text and history.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Takings Clause requires “just compensation” for what property interest state law recognizes as belonging to the owner at the time of the tax-foreclosure transfer, and Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023) frames the historically grounded entitlement as the “overplus” (surplus proceeds) remaining after satisfaction of the tax debt, interest, penalties, and costs—not a constitutional guarantee of fair market value. A categorical fair-market-value rule would improperly constitutionalize routine disputes over the adequacy of state foreclosure-sale procedures and ignore that forced-sale prices differ from arm’s-length market transactions, as BFP v. Resolution Trust Corp. (1994) emphasized. Any claim that the County’s sale mechanics depressed the price is better addressed, if at all, as a process challenge (e.g., due process or state-law compliance) rather than expanding the Fifth Amendment into a federal supervisory regime for tax foreclosures. Nor does the Excessive Fines Clause clearly apply where the government is collecting a delinquent tax obligation through foreclosure rather than imposing a punitive forfeiture, and Tyler itself left such issues largely open.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Fifth Amendment protects the homeowner’s property interest in surplus home equity, and Tyler v. Hennepin County makes clear the government may not satisfy a modest tax debt by confiscating value beyond what is owed simply because state procedures label the excess as forfeited. A categorical rule equating “just compensation” with whatever “surplus proceeds” remain after the county’s chosen sale process risks undercompensating owners where forced-sale mechanics predictably depress price, contrary to the Takings Clause’s command of “just compensation” and the principle that compensation cannot be defined by the government’s own valuation choices. While BFP v. Resolution Trust Corp. addressed fraudulent-transfer avoidance in bankruptcy and does not constitutionalize tax-foreclosure sale prices as “value” for Takings purposes, Tyler’s recognition of an independent equity interest requires the county to account for that interest rather than treat it as extinguished. And where the county retains substantial equity far out of proportion to the delinquency, Tyler’s concurring opinions underscore that an Eighth Amendment Excessive Fines inquiry may be warranted because the equity retention functions as a punitive economic exaction tied to noncompliance with tax law.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Tyler v. Hennepin County holds that a taxpayer retains a protected property interest in home equity beyond the tax debt and that the government violates the Fifth Amendment when it keeps that excess value; that principle forecloses the Sixth Circuit’s categorical rule equating constitutional compensation with whatever “surplus proceeds” remain after the county’s chosen sale mechanics. BFP v. Resolution Trust Corp. addressed “reasonably equivalent value” in bankruptcy fraudulent-transfer law and does not translate into a across-the-board constitutional valuation rule for takings in tax-foreclosure settings, particularly where the State’s process may systematically depress price and thereby define away the owner’s equity. The workable middle ground is to reject the categorical surplus-proceeds rule and require some constitutionally adequate accounting for the owner’s equity interest, while leaving on remand the precise metric and any process-sensitive valuation issues (and any Excessive Fines theory) for development under the Fifth and Eighth Amendments. That approach respects statutory and historical coherence recognized in Tyler and avoids constitutionalizing every state-law procedural complaint while still preventing uncompensated confiscation of surplus equity.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Fifth Amendment’s Takings Clause protects the owner’s equity interest in real property; under Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023), the government may collect delinquent taxes, interest, and costs, but it may not confiscate and retain value beyond what is owed. A categorical rule equating “just compensation” with whatever “surplus proceeds” happen to remain after the government’s chosen sale process cannot be squared with that principle, especially where state law extinguishes title and any residual equity (as Michigan’s scheme did), leaving the owner with nothing despite substantial value. History and early authorities reflect a no-forfeiture-of-surplus understanding in tax collection (see also United States v. Lawton (1884)), confirming that the equity is a cognizable property interest the government must account for. Because the Sixth Circuit relied on BFP’s foreclosure-sale logic in a materially different context and did not develop the historically grounded limits on tax-collection forfeiture, the proper disposition is to reject the categorical “surplus equals value” rule and require compensation for the taken equity (with any Excessive Fines question left for consideration on remand if properly preserved).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023) unanimously held, on history-and-tradition grounds, that a homeowner retains a protected property interest in home equity (the surplus beyond taxes, interest, penalties, and costs) and that the government effects a Fifth Amendment taking when it keeps that value rather than returning it. Isabella County’s categorical rule—treating whatever its chosen foreclosure-sale process yields as the constitutional measure of “just compensation”—overreads BFP v. Resolution Trust Corp. (1994), which addressed a bankruptcy fraudulent-transfer question and did not purport to define the Fifth Amendment’s compensation requirement for tax foreclosures or to authorize equity destruction through depressed or delayed sales. Consistent with Tyler and Michigan’s own recognition of a post-foreclosure equity interest in Rafaeli, LLC v. Oakland County (Mich. 2020), the Constitution requires compensation tied to the owner’s retained equity interest, not merely “surplus proceeds” as defined by the county’s mechanics. The Excessive Fines question is closer, but where the government retains value far beyond what makes it whole, that retention can plausibly operate as punitive and disproportionate under the Eighth Amendment framework discussed in Austin and Timbs (and echoed in Tyler’s concurrence), warranting at least careful scrutiny rather than categorical rejection.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Tyler v. Hennepin County held only that a homeowner retains a cognizable property interest in surplus equity that the State may not simply declare away, but it expressly did not decide how “just compensation” must be calculated (fair market value versus sale-derived surplus). Given that Tyler left valuation open and the Sixth Circuit applied a categorical rule influenced by BFP v. Resolution Trust Corp. treating the foreclosure-sale price as strong evidence of value in forced-sale contexts, I would not adopt Petitioner’s proposed constitutional mandate of fair-market-value compensation on this record. The proper course—consistent with methodological restraint and respect for precedent—is to treat the owner’s constitutional entitlement as the surplus (if any) over the tax debt and associated lawful charges, while leaving process-based objections (including sale mechanics and timing) to due process or state-law channels, and declining to extend the Excessive Fines Clause absent a clear showing of punitive purpose beyond tax collection under the Eighth Amendment.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Tyler v. Hennepin County, 598 U.S. 631 (2023), makes clear that after the tax debt, penalties, and costs are satisfied, the homeowner retains a protected property interest in the remaining equity, so the County cannot redefine the taken property as merely whatever “surplus proceeds” its chosen sale process happens to generate. Under the Fifth Amendment, “just compensation” generally tracks the fair market value of what was taken at the time of the taking (see United States v. New River Collieries Co., 262 U.S. 341 (1923); Jacobs v. United States, 290 U.S. 13 (1933)), and a categorical rule equating auction outcomes with constitutional value—especially in a forced-sale context—risks systematically undercompensating owners and insulating unfair procedures from meaningful review. BFP v. Resolution Trust Corp. (1994) does not control this constitutional question because it addressed the meaning of “reasonably equivalent value” in bankruptcy, not the Fifth Amendment’s compensation requirement for a governmental taking of equity. Additionally, where the government retains substantial equity far beyond the tax delinquency, Tyler’s concurrence (Gorsuch & Jackson, JJ.) underscores that the Excessive Fines Clause may be implicated if the retention functions as a punitive, grossly disproportional exaction rather than mere debt collection.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a county that forecloses and sells a home to satisfy a small unpaid property-tax debt may constitutionally treat the auction price (and/or only the net surplus proceeds) as the property’s value—thereby keeping the owner’s equity—or whether the Fifth and/or Eighth Amendments require returning value beyond what the county paid out as “surplus proceeds.”
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. V (Takings Clause: 'nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation'); U.S. Const. amend. VIII (Excessive Fines Clause, as incorporated against the States).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that the county took far more than was necessary to satisfy the $2,241.93 tax debt by foreclosing on and selling a property with a fair market value alleged to be $194,400 for $76,008, and that the Constitution requires compensation for the owner’s equity rather than letting the county effectively capture it through the tax-foreclosure mechanism. Petitioner and supporting amici contend the Sixth Circuit used a flawed bright-line valuation rule (treating the tax-foreclosure sale price/surplus-proceeds outcome as categorically establishing value) and failed to grapple with Tyler’s implications that owners retain a protected property interest in surplus/equity; they also press, in the alternative, that keeping the equity functions as an excessive fine because it is grossly disproportionate to the underlying tax delinquency.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent county argues that the Constitution is satisfied once the sale occurs under the state’s tax-foreclosure scheme and any 'surplus proceeds' (as determined under that scheme) are handled accordingly; it defends the Sixth Circuit’s approach that the auction result is the best (or controlling) evidence of value, invoking the logic of foreclosure-sale valuation (including reliance on BFP-style reasoning) and emphasizing administrability/finality of tax collection. On the Eighth Amendment issue, the county maintains the equity-retention mechanism is not a punitive 'fine' (or is not excessive under the applicable test), and that any objections about the sales process or sequence of collection steps are better framed as procedural/due-process complaints rather than Takings/Excessive Fines violations.
key_precedents: United States v. Bajakajian (1998) (Excessive Fines proportionality framework, implicated by the Eighth Amendment arguments)

John Roberts.reasoning: The strongest opposing point is Justice Alito’s administrability concern—if we recognize residual equity, do we force fair-market-value litigation in every tax foreclosure—but that risk is overstated if we decide narrowly: the Sixth Circuit erred in treating BFP’s forced-sale price as a categorical Fifth Amendment safe harbor, and the case should return for a Tyler-consistent inquiry focused on whether the government retained value beyond the tax debt and lawful costs. Justice Kagan’s point is dispositive on precedent: BFP construed a bankruptcy statute’s “reasonably equivalent value,” not the Constitution’s “just compensation,” and it did not purport to constitutionalize depressed forced-sale prices. Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas reinforce that while state law helps identify the baseline property interest, a State cannot define away a historically grounded surplus-equity interest by making its own collection mechanism determinative of “value.” On minimalist and legitimacy grounds, we should reverse or vacate and remand without reaching any Eighth Amendment issue or announcing an across-the-board FMV reappraisal rule.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest respondent-side point is Justice Alito’s administrability concern and his premise that state law supplies the full baseline for property interests, but under the original public meaning of the Takings Clause the State’s power to collect taxes by sale never included a power to confiscate the owner’s residual equity as a windfall once the debt and lawful charges are satisfied. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, we can answer administrability without constitutionalizing FMV appraisals in every case by rejecting only the Sixth Circuit’s categorical rule that the forced-sale price is always “just compensation” and remanding for a Tyler-consistent inquiry into any value retained beyond the public charge. Justice Kagan is also right that BFP’s “reasonably equivalent value” holding was bankruptcy-statute specific and cannot be transposed into a Fifth Amendment safe harbor that lets the government’s own chosen process define both what is taken and what it is worth. Michigan’s definitional drafting cannot erase the historically recognized surplus-equity stick in the bundle, so the judgment should be reversed or vacated and remanded.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is administrability: a rule that invites fair-market-value relitigation in every tax foreclosure could destabilize tax collection and swamp courts. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, we can avoid that by doing something narrower—rejecting the Sixth Circuit’s categorical BFP-based premise that a forced-sale price is constitutionally dispositive—and remanding for a Tyler-consistent inquiry limited to whether the government retained value beyond the tax debt and lawful costs. Justice Thomas is also right that BFP interpreted a bankruptcy statute’s “reasonably equivalent value,” not the Fifth Amendment’s “just compensation,” so treating it as a constitutional safe harbor is a category error. Tyler affects my earlier state-law hesitation by clarifying that States cannot define away the historically grounded surplus-equity interest through the mechanics of their own collection scheme; that makes the Sixth Circuit’s bright-line rule untenable even on a conservative, consequence-sensitive approach.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is Justice Alito’s administrability concern: we should not constitutionalize a fair-market-value appraisal fight in every foreclosure. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, the Sixth Circuit’s categorical auction-price-as-value rule goes too far because it lets the State’s forced-sale mechanics define away the very residual equity interest Tyler recognizes as historically protected; a narrow remand can reject that categorical safe harbor without imposing an across-the-board FMV regime. BFP does not undermine this conclusion because, as Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh stress, it interpreted bankruptcy’s “reasonably equivalent value,” not the Fifth Amendment’s measure of just compensation when the government retains a windfall beyond the debt and lawful costs. A Tyler-consistent, fact-sensitive inquiry best protects vulnerable owners from equity stripping while keeping the remedy administrable and cabined.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is Justice Alito’s administrability concern: we should not constitutionalize a fair-market-value appraisal fight in every tax foreclosure. But as the Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Tyler draws a line between using state law to identify the baseline interest and letting a State define away the historically grounded residual equity interest by making its own forced-sale mechanics dispositive; the Sixth Circuit’s BFP-based categorical rule does the latter. Justice Kavanaugh is also right that BFP construed a bankruptcy statute’s “reasonably equivalent value,” not the Fifth Amendment’s “just compensation,” so it cannot supply a safe harbor for government retention of value beyond the debt and lawful costs. The narrow, pragmatic remedy is to reject the auction-price-equals-compensation bright line and remand for a Tyler-consistent inquiry into whether the County kept surplus value, without reaching the Eighth Amendment.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The strongest respondent-side point remains Justice Alito’s administrability concern: we should not constitutionalize routine fair-market-value appraisals in every tax foreclosure. But as the Chief Justice explains, we can answer that concern by rejecting only the Sixth Circuit’s categorical rule that the government’s forced-sale price is dispositive of “just compensation” and remanding for a Tyler-consistent inquiry into whether the County retained value beyond the tax debt and lawful costs. Justice Barrett is also right that BFP construed a bankruptcy statute’s “reasonably equivalent value,” and importing that safe harbor into the Fifth Amendment would let the government define both the taking and the valuation through its own procedures—an approach Tyler forbids even if state law supplies the baseline property interest. On a textualist and originalist view, the sovereign may collect what it is owed, but it may not transmute collection into confiscation of surplus equity via definitional drafting, so reversal/vacatur and remand is the proper narrow disposition.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is Justice Alito’s administrability concern: we should not constitutionalize a fair-market-value appraisal dispute in every tax foreclosure. But the Sixth Circuit’s BFP-based categorical rule goes too far by making the State’s own forced-sale mechanics conclusive of “value,” effectively allowing the government to define away any residual equity interest and retain potential windfalls. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, BFP construed bankruptcy’s “reasonably equivalent value” and does not supply a Fifth Amendment safe harbor, especially after Tyler’s insistence that history and tradition protect surplus equity beyond the debt and lawful costs. The narrow, institutional course is to vacate/reverse the categorical rule and remand for a Tyler-consistent inquiry without reaching the Eighth Amendment.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is administrability: that rejecting the foreclosure-sale price as dispositive will constitutionalize fair-market-value appraisal disputes in routine tax foreclosures. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, we can answer that concern narrowly by holding only that the Sixth Circuit erred in treating BFP as a categorical Fifth Amendment safe harbor, and remand for a Tyler-consistent inquiry focused on whether the government retained value beyond the tax debt and lawful costs. Tyler forecloses the notion—implicit in the Sixth Circuit’s approach—that a State may make its chosen collection mechanism define the constitutional “value” of what it takes, because that would allow the State to redefine away the historically grounded residual equity interest. Justice Alito’s partial shift underscores the point: even taking state-law baselines seriously, state-law labels and sale procedures cannot be constitutionally dispositive where they risk windfall retention forbidden by the Takings Clause.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The strongest respondent-side point remains Justice Alito’s administrability concern—i.e., that recognizing residual equity would constitutionalize fair-market-value fights in every tax foreclosure—but that worry cannot justify a categorical rule that makes the State’s forced-sale mechanism dispositive of constitutional value. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, BFP interpreted a bankruptcy statute’s “reasonably equivalent value” and cannot be transposed into a Fifth Amendment safe harbor without collapsing the property-interest and compensation inquiries into the government’s own process, inviting the very windfall Tyler forbids. A pragmatic, procedurally fair path is to reject the Sixth Circuit’s bright-line auction-price-equals-compensation rule and remand for a Tyler-consistent inquiry into whether the County retained value beyond the tax debt and lawful costs, while making clear we are not mandating routine reappraisals in every case. This approach respects state-law baselines yet preserves meaningful federal scrutiny where the State’s collection process risks stripping surplus equity from owners least able to protect themselves.

John Roberts.reasoning: Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023) squarely holds that a taxpayer retains a protected property interest in home equity beyond the amount necessary to satisfy the tax debt and that the government violates the Fifth Amendment when it keeps that surplus as a windfall rather than providing just compensation. The Sixth Circuit’s categorical rule—treating the foreclosure auction result (or the statutory “surplus proceeds” framework) as conclusively establishing value—reads Tyler too narrowly and improperly forecloses fact-bound inquiries into whether the State has in substance taken equity it must return; BFP v. Resolution Trust Corp. (1994) does not control because it addressed “reasonably equivalent value” in bankruptcy, not “just compensation” for a taking. To protect institutional legitimacy and adhere to precedent while deciding narrowly, I would reverse the categorical valuation rule and remand for application of Tyler’s property-interest framework to determine what equity, if any, was taken without compensation, without reaching the Eighth Amendment issue. This disposition respects federalism by leaving Michigan’s collection mechanisms intact so long as they provide a meaningful avenue to return surplus value consistent with the Takings Clause.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Fifth Amendment’s text forbids the government from taking “private property” without “just compensation,” and under the original public meaning reflected in English/common-law and early American practice—recognized in Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023)—a delinquent taxpayer retained a property interest in surplus value beyond the tax debt and lawful costs. Michigan cannot redefine away that retained equity by deeming the auction price (or only administratively defined “surplus proceeds”) to be the property’s full value; a forced tax sale is a collection mechanism, not a valuation rule that extinguishes the owner’s preexisting property interest. BFP v. Resolution Trust Corp. (1994) concerned bankruptcy/fraudulent-transfer valuation and does not control the distinct constitutional question whether the State may keep an owner’s equity after satisfying the public charge. Because Tyler establishes that surplus equity is constitutionally protected property, the County’s retention of value beyond the tax obligation effects an uncompensated taking in violation of the Takings Clause (without needing to reach the Eighth Amendment).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Takings Clause requires “just compensation” only for property interests the owner retains under state law, and after Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023) the key question is whether Michigan law recognizes a continuing property interest in the retained equity beyond any statutory “surplus proceeds,” which the Sixth Circuit did not fully analyze under history and tradition. I would not extend BFP v. Resolution Trust Corp. (1994) beyond its bankruptcy context to create a categorical constitutional rule that the foreclosure-sale price always equals “just compensation,” but I also doubt the Eighth Amendment applies because retention of value through a tax-collection foreclosure scheme is not obviously punitive in the sense of an “excessive fine” under Bajakajian. Given the administrability and law-enforcement/tax-collection interests at stake, and absent a clearly established state-law property entitlement to additional equity, the county’s approach is constitutionally permissible, at least on this record. Accordingly, I would vote to affirm the judgment for the county.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023) makes clear that a homeowner retains a protected property interest in home equity/surplus value beyond the tax debt, and the Fifth Amendment’s Takings Clause forbids the government from using tax collection as a pretext to appropriate that interest without just compensation. The Sixth Circuit’s categorical rule equating the foreclosure-auction result (or state-defined “surplus proceeds”) with constitutional “value” improperly allows the County to capture equity—especially where the sale price may reflect procedural distortions rather than fair value—and is in tension with Tyler’s rejection of windfall retention. BFP v. Resolution Trust Corp. (1994) does not control because it addressed bankruptcy “reasonably equivalent value” in mortgage foreclosures, not whether a State may define away an owner’s residual property interest for Takings purposes after satisfying a small tax debt. Given the real-world impact on vulnerable homeowners and the mismatch between a $2,241.93 debt and the loss of substantial equity, the Constitution requires returning value beyond what is needed to make the County whole (and, if necessary on remand, courts may also consider whether the equity confiscation operates as an excessive and grossly disproportionate penalty under the Eighth Amendment framework of Bajakajian).
